---
title: "String"
description: "From letter tiles to java.lang.String: characters as numbers, UTF-16 code units versus code points, immutability, why += in a loop costs n(n+1)/2 copies and StringBuilder does not, palindromes, counting arrays for anagrams, lexicographic order, and hard interview problems solved math-first."
---

A string is an array of characters with two twists. In Java it can never change once made, and its "characters" are 16-bit code units, which do not always match what a human calls a character. This lesson starts from letters as numbers, counts exactly what immutability costs, and finishes with palindrome and parenthesis problems solved by counting.

All code is in [`StringLab.java`](StringLab.java). Run it from this folder with `java StringLab.java`; it checks every number on this page and prints `OK`.

## The problem

A word game receives the words `eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat` and must put words made of the same letters into the same group: `{eat, tea, ate}`, `{tan, nat}`, `{bat}`.

- Comparing every pair of words, and for each pair trying every rearrangement of letters, is hopeless: a 10-letter word has $10! = 3{,}628{,}800$ rearrangements.
- Building each group by gluing strings together with `+=` looks innocent but copies the whole string again on every step.
- The right tool is to see letters as **numbers**: `'a'` is 97, so `c - 'a'` turns a letter into an index from 0 to 25, and a word becomes a tally of 26 counts. Two words belong together exactly when their tallies are equal.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip}
A string is a row of letter tiles on a Scrabble rack. Each tile sits in a numbered position, 0, 1, 2, and so on, so "the tile in position 2" is found at once, just like an array.

A Java `String` is more like a **printed name badge** than a rack. You cannot pick a letter off a badge. To change "jave" into "java" you print a whole new badge, and the old one is still there for anyone who was holding it. That sounds wasteful, but it means a badge you hand to a friend can never be changed behind your back. Joshua Bloch's *Effective Java* (3rd edition, Item 17, "Minimize mutability") makes this case for immutable classes, and Item 63, "Beware the performance of string concatenation", warns about the cost: printing a new badge for every added letter.

Two words are **anagrams** when they use the same tiles: pour both racks into piles sorted by letter and the piles match. A **palindrome** reads the same from both ends, like "racecar": point one finger at each end and walk them towards the middle.
:::

## From simple to advanced

### Level 1: a string is a sequence with positions

A string of length $n$ is a sequence $s = s_0 s_1 \dots s_{n-1}$. Java's `s.charAt(i)` reads $s_i$ in $O(1)$, and `s.substring(i, j)` returns the piece $s_i \dots s_{j-1}$, of length $j - i$. The number of non-empty substrings is

$$
\#\text{substrings} = \binom{n + 1}{2} = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}
$$

where:

- $n$ is the length of the string;
- a substring is fixed by choosing a start $i$ and an end $j$ with $0 \le i < j \le n$, which is choosing 2 of the $n + 1$ cut points;
- $\binom{n+1}{2}$ is "$n + 1$ choose 2".

Example: `"java"` has $n = 4$, so $\frac{4 \times 5}{2} = 10$ substrings: 4 of length 1, 3 of length 2, 2 of length 3 and 1 of length 4. Only 9 are different, because `"a"` appears twice. A brute force that examines every substring and spends $O(n)$ on each is therefore $O(n^3)$; the interview problems below avoid that.

Every Java `String` is **immutable**. `word.toUpperCase()` does not touch `word`; it returns a new string:

| Call | `word` afterwards | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `word = "java"` | `"java"` | |
| `word.toUpperCase()` | still `"java"` | a new string `"JAVA"` |

Immutability lets strings be shared freely, used safely as `HashMap` keys, and cache their hash code (`String` keeps it in a private `hash` field after computing it once). Since Java 9 ([JEP 254, Compact Strings](https://openjdk.org/jeps/254)), a string whose characters all fit in one byte is even stored as one byte per character.

### Level 2: characters are numbers, and UTF-16

A Java `char` is a 16-bit number, a **UTF-16 code unit**. `'a'` is 97, `'b'` is 98, and so on to `'z'` = 122, so `c - 'a'` maps the lower-case letters onto $0..25$. That single subtraction is the trick behind every counting array in this lesson.

Sixteen bits give only 65,536 values, but Unicode has over a million **code points**. Code points above `U+FFFF`, such as most emoji, are stored as **two** code units, a *surrogate pair*:

$$
u' = u - \text{0x10000}, \qquad \text{high} = \text{0xD800} + \left\lfloor \frac{u'}{2^{10}} \right\rfloor, \qquad \text{low} = \text{0xDC00} + (u' \bmod 2^{10})
$$

where:

- $u$ is the code point, a number from `0x10000` to `0x10FFFF`;
- $u'$ is what is left after removing the first 65,536 values; it fits in 20 bits;
- the high surrogate carries the top 10 bits and the low surrogate the bottom 10 bits;
- `0x` marks hexadecimal, so `0x10000` is 65,536 and $2^{10} = 1024$.

Example: the grinning face 😀 is $u = \text{0x1F600} = 128{,}512$.

- $u' = 128{,}512 - 65{,}536 = 62{,}976$ (`0xF600`);
- $\lfloor 62{,}976 / 1024 \rfloor = 61$ (`0x3D`), so high $= \text{0xD800} + \text{0x3D} = \text{0xD83D}$;
- $62{,}976 - 61 \times 1024 = 512$ (`0x200`), so low $= \text{0xDC00} + \text{0x200} = \text{0xDE00}$.

So `"😀".length()` is **2**, while `"😀".codePointCount(0, 2)` is **1**.

```java
static char[] surrogatePair(int codePoint) {
    int offset = codePoint - 0x10000;      // 20 bits remain
    char high = (char) (0xD800 + (offset >> 10));
    char low = (char) (0xDC00 + (offset & 0x3FF));
    return new char[] {high, low};
}
```

Most interview strings are plain `a`–`z`, so `char` indexing is fine there. In real text, `charAt` can split an emoji in half. Use `codePoints()` to walk real characters; `StringBuilder.reverse()` already keeps surrogate pairs together.

### Level 3: building strings, `+=` versus `StringBuilder`

Because a `String` cannot grow, `s += "a"` creates a **new** string of length $\lvert s \rvert + 1$ and copies every character into it. Appending one character $n$ times copies

$$
1 + 2 + \dots + n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}
$$

where:

- $n$ is the number of appends;
- the $i$-th append builds a string of length $i$, copying $i$ characters;
- the sum is the triangular number, which grows like $n^2 / 2$.

Example: 5 appends copy $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$ characters. For $n = 10{,}000$ that is $\frac{10{,}000 \times 10{,}001}{2} = 50{,}005{,}000$ characters, to build a string of only 10,000.

```java
static int charactersCopiedByPlusEquals(int n) {
    String s = "";
    int copied = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        s += "a";                          // a new string of length i + 1, every character copied
        copied += s.length();
    }
    return copied;
}
```

`StringBuilder` is a growable character array, exactly the `ArrayList` idea from the [Array](../array/index.qmd) lesson. It starts with room for 16 and, when full, grows from capacity $c$ to $2c + 2$ (OpenJDK `AbstractStringBuilder.newCapacity`):

$$
\text{total copies} = \sum_{j} c_j < 2n
$$

where:

- $c_j$ is the capacity at the $j$-th resize, $c_0 = 16$ and $c_{j+1} = 2 c_j + 2$;
- each resize copies the $c_j$ characters already present;
- each capacity is less than half the next, so the sum is less than twice the last capacity, which is below $n$.

Example: 10,000 appends resize at $16, 34, 70, 142, 286, 574, 1150, 2302, 4606, 9214$, copying $18{,}394 < 20{,}000$ characters. That is 18 thousand instead of 50 million.

```java
static String repeatWithBuilder(char c, int n) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sb.append(c);  // writes into spare room; grows about 2x when full
    return sb.toString();
}
```

A single line such as `"x = " + x + "!"` is fine: the compiler builds it in one go. The trap is `+=` **inside a loop**.

### Level 4: palindromes, reading from both ends

A string is a palindrome when each character equals its mirror image:

$$
\operatorname{pal}(s) \iff s_i = s_{n-1-i} \text{ for all } 0 \le i < \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor
$$

where:

- $n$ is the length;
- $s_{n-1-i}$ is the character $i$ places from the end;
- $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ pairs are enough: the middle character of an odd-length string is its own mirror.

Example: `"racecar"`, $n = 7$, needs $\lfloor 7/2 \rfloor = 3$ comparisons: $s_0 = s_6 = $ `r`, $s_1 = s_5 = $ `a`, $s_2 = s_4 = $ `c`. All equal, so it is a palindrome. `"rocket"` fails at the first pair, `r` against `t`.

```java
static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
    for (int i = 0, j = s.length() - 1; i < j; i++, j--) {
        if (s.charAt(i) != s.charAt(j)) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
```

### Level 5: anagrams, counting with an array

Two strings are anagrams exactly when every letter occurs equally often in both:

$$
s \sim t \iff \operatorname{cnt}_s(c) = \operatorname{cnt}_t(c) \text{ for every letter } c \in \lbrace \texttt{a}, \dots, \texttt{z} \rbrace
$$

where:

- $\sim$ means "is an anagram of";
- $\operatorname{cnt}_s(c)$ is how many times letter $c$ occurs in $s$;
- the 26 counts live in an `int[26]`, at index $c - \texttt{'a'}$.

Example: `"listen"` and `"silent"` both have one each of `e, i, l, n, s, t` and zero of the other 20 letters, so they are anagrams. `"rat"` and `"car"` differ at `t` (1 against 0), so they are not.

```java
static int[] letterCounts(String s) {
    int[] count = new int[26];
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) count[c - 'a']++;  // 'a' -> 0, 'b' -> 1, ..., 'z' -> 25
    return count;
}

static boolean isAnagram(String s, String t) {
    return Arrays.equals(letterCounts(s), letterCounts(t));
}
```

This costs $O(n)$, compared with $O(n \log n)$ for sorting both strings and comparing. A counting array is direct addressing from the [Hash Table](../hash-table/index.qmd) lesson, with a universe of only 26 keys.

### Level 6: comparing strings

`s.equals(t)` compares letters. `s == t` asks whether they are the **same object**, which depends on how they were built: a string assembled by `StringBuilder` is a different object from the literal `"java"`, even though the letters match.

For ordering, Java uses **lexicographic** (dictionary) order. Find the first position where the strings differ:

$$
\operatorname{cmp}(s, t) =
\begin{cases}
s_k - t_k & \text{if } k = \min \lbrace i : s_i \ne t_i \rbrace \text{ exists} \\
\lvert s \rvert - \lvert t \rvert & \text{if one string is a prefix of the other}
\end{cases}
$$

where:

- $k$ is the first index where the two strings disagree;
- $s_k - t_k$ is the difference of the two character codes;
- $\lvert s \rvert$ is the length of $s$; a negative result means $s$ comes first.

Example: `"apple".compareTo("apply")` first differs at $k = 4$, `e` against `y`: $101 - 121 = -20$, so "apple" comes first. `"app".compareTo("apple")` has no differing position, so it returns $3 - 5 = -2$. Only the sign is promised by the `Comparable` contract, so test `< 0`, never `== -1`.

## Why it works and what it costs

**Palindrome check.** The invariant is: *when the loop reaches positions $i$ and $j = n - 1 - i$, every earlier pair has matched.* If some pair fails, the string is not a palindrome. If $i$ meets or passes $j$, all $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ pairs matched, which is exactly the definition.

**Anagram check.** Rearranging letters changes their positions but never their counts, so anagrams have equal count arrays. Conversely, equal counts let you rebuild $t$ by taking the letters of $s$ in a different order, so equal counts imply anagrams. The counting array is therefore a *canonical form*: one representative per group.

**Costs**, for strings of length $n$:

| Operation | Cost | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `charAt(i)`, `length()` | $O(1)$ | array indexing |
| `substring(i, j)`, `toUpperCase()`, `+` | $O(j - i)$ or $O(n)$ | builds and copies a new string |
| `equals`, `compareTo` | $O(n)$ | compares up to the first difference |
| `hashCode()` | $O(n)$ once, then $O(1)$ | cached in the string |
| $n$ appends with `+=` | $O(n^2)$ | $n(n+1)/2$ characters copied |
| $n$ appends with `StringBuilder` | $O(n)$ amortised | fewer than $2n$ characters copied by resizes |
| palindrome, anagram | $O(n)$ | one pass; the anagram tally uses 26 counters |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Comparing with `==` | Equal-looking strings compare as different, sometimes | Use `equals`, or `equalsIgnoreCase` |
| `s += piece` inside a loop | A loop over 100,000 pieces takes seconds | `StringBuilder`, or `String.join` |
| Calling `s.toUpperCase()` and ignoring the result | The string "does not change" | Strings are immutable: `s = s.toUpperCase();` |
| Assuming `length()` counts visible characters | An emoji counts as 2 and `charAt` splits it | `codePointCount`, `codePoints()` |
| `count[c - 'a']` on input with capitals or spaces | `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` (`' ' - 'a'` is $-65$) | Normalise first, or count in a `HashMap` or an `int[128]` |
| Testing `compareTo(...) == -1` | Works for some strings, fails for others | Only the sign is defined: test `< 0` |
| `substring(i, j)` with `j` as a length | Wrong slice or `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` | The second argument is the end index, exclusive |

## Interview problems

Each solution starts with the mathematics. Once the formula is right, the code is short.

### 1. LeetCode 49: Group Anagrams (Medium)

**Problem.** Group the words that are anagrams of each other, in any order. For `["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]` the answer is `[["bat"], ["nat", "tan"], ["ate", "eat", "tea"]]`.

**Math first.** Map each word to a key that is equal exactly for anagrams. Level 5 says the count vector is such a key:

$$
\operatorname{key}(w) = \big(\operatorname{cnt}_w(\texttt{a}), \operatorname{cnt}_w(\texttt{b}), \dots, \operatorname{cnt}_w(\texttt{z})\big), \qquad w \sim v \iff \operatorname{key}(w) = \operatorname{key}(v)
$$

where:

- $w$ and $v$ are words;
- $\operatorname{key}(w)$ is a vector of 26 counts;
- each group is the set of words sharing one key.

Example: $\operatorname{key}(\text{eat}) = \operatorname{key}(\text{tea}) = \operatorname{key}(\text{ate})$, with a 1 at `a`, `e` and `t` and 0 elsewhere. $\operatorname{key}(\text{tan}) = \operatorname{key}(\text{nat})$ has 1 at `a`, `n`, `t`. $\operatorname{key}(\text{bat})$ has 1 at `a`, `b`, `t`. Three distinct keys give three groups.

**Idea.** Use a `HashMap` from key to list of words. `Arrays.toString(count)` turns the 26 counts into a string such as `"[1, 0, 0, 0, 1, ...]"`, which has proper `equals` and `hashCode`, unlike a raw `int[]`.

```java
static List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] words) {
    Map<String, List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
    for (String w : words) {
        String key = Arrays.toString(letterCounts(w));    // equal counts, equal key
        groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(w);
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(groups.values());
}
```

**Answer.** Three groups: `{bat}`, `{nat, tan}`, `{ate, eat, tea}`. For $m$ words of length at most $k$, building keys costs $O(m(k + 26))$; for the example, $6 \times (3 + 26) = 174$ steps. Space is $O(mk)$. Sorting each word as its key would cost $O(m \cdot k \log k)$ instead.

### 2. LeetCode 5: Longest Palindromic Substring (Medium)

**Problem.** Return the longest substring that is a palindrome. For `"babad"` the answer is `"bab"` (`"aba"` is also accepted); for `"cbbd"` it is `"bb"`.

**Math first.** Every palindrome has a centre: a character (odd length) or a gap between two characters (even length). A string of length $n$ has

$$
\#\text{centres} = n + (n - 1) = 2n - 1, \qquad \text{work} \le \sum_{\text{centres}} \left\lceil \frac{n}{2} \right\rceil = O(n^2)
$$

where:

- $n$ centres sit on characters and $n - 1$ sit in the gaps between neighbours;
- from each centre, expansion compares $s_{lo}$ with $s_{hi}$ and steps outwards while they match;
- one expansion can grow at most halfway across the string.

Example: `"babad"`, $n = 5$, has $2 \times 5 - 1 = 9$ centres. From the centre at index 1 (`a`): $s_0 = s_2 = $ `b` matches, then $lo = -1$ stops it, giving `"bab"`, length 3. No centre does better, so the answer has length **3**. In `"cbbd"` the gap between the two `b`s expands to `"bb"`, length 2.

**Idea.** For each index $c$ try two expansions: from $(c, c)$ for odd lengths and from $(c, c+1)$ for even lengths. `expand` returns the length found; the start is then $c - \lfloor (\text{length} - 1)/2 \rfloor$.

```java
static String longestPalindrome(String s) {
    int start = 0, end = 0;                // the best palindrome so far is s[start..end)
    for (int c = 0; c < s.length(); c++) {
        int length = Math.max(expand(s, c, c), expand(s, c, c + 1));  // odd and even centres
        if (length > end - start) {
            start = c - (length - 1) / 2;
            end = start + length;
        }
    }
    return s.substring(start, end);
}

static int expand(String s, int lo, int hi) {      // length of the palindrome grown from s[lo..hi]
    while (lo >= 0 && hi < s.length() && s.charAt(lo) == s.charAt(hi)) {
        lo--;
        hi++;
    }
    return hi - lo - 1;
}
```

**Answer.** `"bab"` for `"babad"`, `"bb"` for `"cbbd"`, `"a"` for `"a"`. $O(n^2)$ time in the worst case, such as `"aaaa…"`, and $O(1)$ extra space. Manacher's algorithm reaches $O(n)$ by reusing mirror information, but is rarely expected in an interview.

### 3. LeetCode 32: Longest Valid Parentheses (Hard)

**Problem.** Given a string of `(` and `)`, return the length of the longest well-formed substring. For `")()())"` the answer is 4, from `"()()"`.

**Math first.** Give `(` the value $+1$ and `)` the value $-1$, and let $B$ be the running sum over a stretch of characters. A stretch is well-formed exactly when

$$
B_{\text{end}} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad B_m \ge 0 \text{ at every point } m \text{ along the way}
$$

where:

- $B_m$ is (opens so far) minus (closes so far), counted from the start of the stretch;
- $B_m < 0$ means a `)` with no partner, so no valid stretch can extend across that point;
- $B_{\text{end}} = 0$ means every `(` has been closed.

Example: `")()())"`. Start a stretch at each reset:

| Character | `)` | `(` | `)` | `(` | `)` | `)` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| opens, closes | 0, 1 → reset | 1, 0 | 1, 1 | 2, 1 | 2, 2 | 2, 3 → reset |
| balanced length | | | **2** | | **4** | |

The best balanced length is $2 \times 2 = 4$.

**Idea.** Keep two counters and scan left to right. Whenever they are equal, $2 \times \text{closes}$ is a candidate; whenever closes exceed opens, reset both. A left-to-right scan never sees $B = 0$ in `"(()"`, because the extra `(` keeps opens ahead. So also scan the reversed string with the roles of `(` and `)` swapped.

```java
static int longestValidParentheses(String s) {
    String reversed = new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString();
    return Math.max(scan(s, '('), scan(reversed, ')'));
}

static int scan(String s, char open) {     // longest balanced run, reading left to right
    int opens = 0, closes = 0, best = 0;
    for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (ch == open) opens++;
        else closes++;
        if (opens == closes) best = Math.max(best, 2 * closes);
        else if (closes > opens) opens = closes = 0;   // an unmatched closer: start afresh
    }
    return best;
}
```

**Answer.** 4 for `")()())"`; 2 for `"(()"` (the forward pass gives 0, the backward pass gives 2); 6 for `"()(())"`; 0 for `""`. Two passes of $n$ steps: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space apart from the reversed copy. The classic alternative keeps a stack of indices of unmatched characters, which is also $O(n)$ but uses $O(n)$ space.

## Mathematical Abstraction

A string is a finite sequence over an alphabet, and most string tricks replace it with a cheaper summary:

$$
s \in \Sigma^n, \qquad \operatorname{cnt}_s : \Sigma \to \mathbb{N}, \qquad \text{cost of } n \text{ appends} =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} & \text{immutable } \texttt{+=} \\[6pt]
< 3n & \texttt{StringBuilder}
\end{cases}
$$

where:

- $\Sigma$ is the alphabet, for example the 26 lower-case letters, and $\Sigma^n$ is the set of strings of length $n$;
- $\operatorname{cnt}_s$ is the count summary: it forgets order and keeps only how often each letter occurs;
- $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of counts $0, 1, 2, \dots$;
- the costs count characters written: $n$ appends plus fewer than $2n$ resize copies for `StringBuilder`.

Example: `"listen"` and `"silent"` are different sequences in $\Sigma^6$ but have the same summary, so they are anagrams. Building a 10,000-character string costs 50,005,000 copies with `+=` but $10{,}000 + 18{,}394 = 28{,}394$ writes with `StringBuilder`, under $3 \times 10{,}000$.
